title: compact-sweep-intent-latency-cost-profiles
body:
Summary:
This is a working draft of a compact benchmark sweep focusing on intent-detection style requests (very short prompts, heavy returned decisions) and comparison of latency and per-conversation cost across model variants, quantization levels, and KV-cache hit scenarios. Goal: give product and solutions engineering a small, actionable matrix for recommended defaults on short-turn, high-QPS inference (chat/intents, bot routing, classification).

Key takeaways (short):
- For <64-token prompts where model outputs are concise (classification/intent labels), p95 latency correlates strongly with batch-formation delay when batching windows >5ms. Small fixed-window batching (<=2ms) with 1-4 request batch sizes gives best p95 under QPS 200–2k.
- 4-bit asymmetric quantization reduces cost by ~28–34% with median latency impact <6% on A100-like hardware; p99 shows wider variance when KV-cache is cold.
- KV-cache hit rate changes the economics: with >85% hit rate, sessionized amortized cost drops 20–40% for multi-turn flows; but for single-turn intents (no follow-on), cache overhead sometimes increases tail latency due to cache lookup lock contention in our prototype.

Methods and testbed:
- Hardware: 1x A100-40GB (node), 1x V100 (legacy reference).
- Serving runtime: local dev build (commit: bench/compact-sweep@f3b9a2) with batching window controls and KV-cache instrumentation enabled.
- Models tested: Redwood-small-7b (float16), Redwood-small-7b (4bit), OpenLLaMA-3b (float16), opt-2.7b (float16).
- Workload: synthetic intent generator (100k unique short prompts, avg 28 tokens). Responses constrained to 8–32 tokens.
- QPS regimes: 50, 200, 800, 2000 sustained. Each run 10 minutes with 2-minute warmup.
- Metrics captured: median/p95/p99 latency (server observed), batching latency (time waiting in queue), kernel-time, token-cost, amortized cost per conversation (USD per 1k convs), KV-cache hit rate.

Micro-results (representative excerpts):
1) Latency vs quantization (QPS 800, no KV-cache):
Model            | p50  | p95  | p99  | batch-avg | kernel-ms
Redwood-7b-fp16  | 28ms | 72ms | 120ms| 3.8ms     | 18ms
Redwood-7b-4bit  | 30ms | 78ms | 150ms| 4.1ms     | 19ms
OpenLLaMA-3b     | 36ms | 110ms| 220ms| 5.3ms     | 24ms

Notes: 4-bit adds small kernel overhead but reduces peak memory pressure enabling slightly denser packing at sustained QPS. p99 divergence is dominated by GC/driver stalls observed in 4-bit path on V100 testing.

2) Cost per 1k conversations (short intents, avg response 16 tokens):
Scenario                          | USD/1k convs
Baseline (fp16, no cache)          | $3.80
4bit (no cache)                   | $2.75
fp16 + high-kv-hit (88%)          | $2.30
4bit + high-kv-hit (88%)         | $1.70

Interpretation: Quantization + effective KV caching multiplies savings. For single-turn intents, KV caching overhead (lookup + lock) may not pay off unless a reuse pattern exists across sessions.

3) Batching window sensitivity for short prompts (Redwood-7b-4bit, QPS 2000):
Batching window | avg-batch-size | p95  | p99
0.5ms           | 1.2            | 38ms | 92ms
2ms             | 1.9            | 45ms | 100ms
5ms             | 3.6            | 60ms | 160ms
10ms            | 6.8            | 92ms | 280ms

Recommendation: keep batching window <=2ms for p95-sensitive routes; allow larger windows for throughput-first endpoints. For user-facing intent detection (p95 <=100ms target), 2ms window is sweet spot under high QPS.

4) KV-cache interplay (sessionized flow with 3 turns average):
- Cold-cache baseline (no reuse): amortized cost ~= baseline above.
- 50% hit: amortized cost drops ~12%; tail latency slightly higher due to lock contention spikes.
- 90% hit: amortized cost drops 30–40%; median latency improves but p99 depends on cache eviction and background serialization events.

Small ASCII heatmap: p95 latency (ms) across QPS x KV-hit (Redwood-7b-4bit)
QPS
     KV  | 50   | 200  | 800  | 2000
     0%  | 42ms | 46ms | 78ms | 100ms
    50%  | 40ms | 44ms | 70ms | 90ms
    88%  | 34ms | 38ms | 60ms | 78ms

Operational notes and caveats:
- Our 4-bit pathway currently uses custom kernels that are not yet in the stable runtime; we observed occasional driver-level timeouts on older GPU setups (V100). Patch scheduled in PR #412 to add a watchdog and backoff.
- KV-cache instrumentation shows pointer-churn in the Go shim. We should consider a lock-free read path or sharded locks for high-QPS routes.
- Cost shown assumes cloud spot pricing equivalent to our internal unit costs; absolute USD should be re-run against customer pricing tiers for quotes.

Actionable recommendations (for product and solutions):
- Default for intent endpoints: Redwood-7b-4bit + batching window 2ms + enable KV-cache only for multi-turn routes where historical telemetry shows >30% reuse within 30s.
- For enterprise customers on Dedicated: offer an \"intent-optimized\" profile that sets small batching windows, quantization to 4-bit, and an analysis tool that flags routes with low cache ROI.
- Add a lightweight per-route simulation to the Console: given historical session traces, estimate p95 and USD/1k convs across three profiles (fp16, 4bit, 4bit+cache) so customers can choose trade-offs.

Open questions / next steps:
- Re-run sweep on multi-node multi-GPU to validate packing improvements at sustained 10k QPS.
- A/B test lock-free cache read path prototype to measure p99 improvement under high contention.
- Add a small-run with on-prem H100 to get upper bound latency numbers.

Appendix: quick checklist for repeats
- commit id, node image, cloud SKU, benchmark flags (seed), prompt generator config, run start/end times, raw traces location (bench server).

Raw artifacts: linked in linked_artifacts above; raw CSVs currently in s3://redwood-bench/compact-sweep/ (internal).

Notes-to-self: verify that token-cost reporting uses model-specific tokenization (open tokenizer sometimes undercounts subword splits). Also check whether our per-request logging truncates prompts longer than 128 tokens (should not affect this sweep but good to standardize).

End of draft.
